title.rendered: How to Write an RFQ for Custom Metal Mesh: The Information Engineers Need

content.rendered:
Custom mesh quotes are slow when the request is vague. A complete RFQ lets engineers recommend a construction, check manufacturability and quote with confidence in one round instead of five.

The checklist

1. Application and duty

  • What is the mesh for: filtration, electrode support, gas diffusion, separation, a protective screen or something else?
  • What fluid or gas will it see, and at what temperature and pressure?
  • What must it retain, pass or conduct?

2. Material

  • Preferred alloy, or the chemical environment so we can recommend one.
  • Any standards or approvals the material must meet.

3. Mesh construction

  • Woven or knitted, if known.
  • Wire diameter, opening size or mesh count, and any porosity or permeability target.

4. Form and dimensions

  • Roll, sheet, disc, tube, cartridge or formed part.
  • Width, length, diameter and thickness, with tolerances.
  • Any corrugation, laser-cut outline or edge treatment.

5. Treatments and cleanliness

  • Annealing, coating, cleaning or other finishing.
  • Cleanliness or contamination limits for sensitive assemblies.

6. Quantity and timeline

  • Prototype, sample, pilot or production volume, and the repeat rate.
  • Required delivery date and packaging requirements.

7. Documents

  • Drawings or sketches, in PDF, STEP, DWG or DXF.
  • Required material certificates, inspection reports and traceability.

If you do not know everything

You do not need to. Tell us the duty and the envelope and our application engineers will propose the rest, including whether woven or knitted is the right route. Early, honest uncertainty is easier to work with than a precise specification that does not match the application.

You can attach drawings and details through the technical RFQ form, or read how we work on engineering and manufacturing.

title.rendered: Annealing, Coating and Surface Treatment of Metal Mesh: What Each Process Does

content.rendered:
Weaving or knitting makes a mesh. Treatment makes it a component. The processes that follow forming decide how the mesh behaves in assembly and in service.

Annealing

Drawing wire and then weaving or knitting it work-hardens the metal. Annealing is a controlled heat treatment that relieves that stress and softens the material.

  • Improves formability, so the mesh can be corrugated or shaped without cracking.
  • Tunes hardness and springback.
  • Gives a more uniform structure across a roll.

The right atmosphere and temperature profile depend on the alloy, so ask your supplier how the furnace is controlled.

Cleaning and surface preparation

Degreasing and cleaning remove drawing lubricants and handling residue. For electrolyser and fuel cell parts, a clean, consistent surface is essential for catalyst adhesion and for keeping contamination out of the cell.

Coating

Coatings add a function the base metal does not have: conductivity, catalytic activity, corrosion protection or a defined surface chemistry. Thickness and pattern control determine whether the coating performs as intended, so they should be specified rather than assumed.

Forming and cutting

  • Corrugation adds stiffness and open channels and can increase effective filter area.
  • Laser cutting produces clean, repeatable edges and complex outlines, with minimal fraying.
  • Slitting and cutting to size turn rolls into the widths and shapes an assembly needs.

Choosing the right sequence

  1. Define what the mesh must do in service.
  2. Decide the form it must take and how it will be assembled.
  3. Select the treatments in an order that does not undo each other, for example anneal before final forming and clean before coating.
  4. Specify inspection for each step.

BVK Hydrotech runs annealing, coating, corrugation and laser cutting alongside weaving and knitting. See process and treatments and engineering and manufacturing.

title.rendered: Metal Mesh in Fuel Cells: Gas Diffusion, Current Collection and Electrode Support

content.rendered:
Fuel cells convert hydrogen back into electricity, and every cell needs gas to reach the catalyst, current to leave the cell and a structure to hold it all together. Metal mesh is used to do each of those jobs.

The three jobs

  • Gas diffusion. A porous layer spreads reactant gas evenly over the electrode and lets product water or gas leave.
  • Current collection. A conductive path carries current from the electrode to the plate.
  • Electrode support. A robust substrate holds the catalyst layer and the membrane assembly in place.

How the design changes by cell type

Cell type Typical environment Mesh considerations
AFC (alkaline) Alkaline electrolyte Nickel-based mesh for caustic compatibility
PEM Acidic, humid, moderate temperature Corrosion-resistant materials such as titanium, with careful surface condition
SOFC High temperature, oxidising High-temperature alloys that keep conductivity and strength

The parameters that matter

  1. Permeability and porosity: set gas distribution and water handling.
  2. Conductivity and contact: low resistance across the stack.
  3. Mechanical strength and springback: keeps contact under clamping load and thermal cycling.
  4. Surface condition and cleanliness: contamination hurts catalyst performance.
  5. Dimensional consistency: every cell in a stack must behave alike.

Why mesh instead of other media

Metal mesh gives designers tight control of porosity, a consistent structure and compatibility with demanding chemistries and temperatures. It can be cut, formed and treated to the exact geometry of the cell.

BVK Hydrotech engineers woven and knitted mesh for gas diffusion, current collection and electrode support in AFC, PEM and SOFC stacks. See fuel cell solutions for the details, and our R&D and CFD prototyping capability for early design work.

title.rendered: Nickel Mesh for Alkaline Water Electrolysis: Grades, Roles and Selection

content.rendered:
Alkaline water electrolysis is the most established route to green hydrogen. It uses a strongly alkaline electrolyte, and nickel is the metal that copes with it best at a sensible cost.

Why nickel

Nickel is highly resistant to caustic solutions, conducts electricity well and supports good catalytic behaviour for the reactions at the electrodes. That combination makes it the default material for electrodes and cell internals in alkaline systems.

Ni 201 versus Ni 202

Both are commercially pure nickel designations. Ni 201 is the low-carbon grade, and the low carbon limit protects it from graphite precipitation and embrittlement at sustained high temperatures. Your supplier should confirm the exact grade and composition that suits your operating window.

Where nickel mesh is used in the cell

  • Electrode substrate. Woven or expanded nickel carries the catalyst coating and offers a large surface.
  • Elastic and current-collecting elements. Knitted or corrugated nickel mesh keeps electrical contact across the stack.
  • Separator support and gas-liquid management. Open mesh layers help bubbles escape and electrolyte circulate.

Selection points

  1. Wire diameter: finer wire gives more surface; thicker wire gives stiffness and life.
  2. Mesh geometry: aperture and weave control porosity and bubble release.
  3. Surface condition: cleanliness matters, and a catalyst coating needs a consistent surface to adhere to.
  4. Annealing: controls hardness and springback.
  5. Form and size: match the cell frame, and prefer fewer joints in the active area.

Beyond the mesh

Traceability matters in a component that is expected to run for years. Ask for batch and material documentation. Our electrolyser solutions page covers the materials and processes BVK Hydrotech applies, and the knitted mesh in electrolysers article explains the elastic-element role.

title.rendered: Knitted Metal Mesh in Green Hydrogen Electrolysers: Where It Fits and Why

content.rendered:
Green hydrogen depends on electrolysers that run efficiently for years. Inside the stack, a surprising amount of that performance rests on the metal mesh between the plates.

What knitted mesh does in a stack

  • Elastic element. The springy, compressible structure keeps electrical contact between cell components while absorbing tolerance and thermal movement.
  • Gas diffusion and porous transport. An open, permeable structure lets gas bubbles leave and liquid reach the electrode surface.
  • Current collection. A continuous metallic path carries current across the active area.
  • Separator and balance-of-plant filtration. Mesh can also act as a separator layer and as a filter in the surrounding system.

Why knitted rather than woven

Knitted loops can compress and recover. That elasticity maintains contact pressure across a large active area, which a rigid woven cloth cannot do as well. Knitting can also produce large single pieces and corrugated forms that are difficult to build from cut cloth.

What to specify

  1. Material: nickel for alkaline cells; titanium for acidic PEM cells; stainless steel where the chemistry allows.
  2. Wire diameter and density: these set stiffness, porosity and contact behaviour.
  3. Single or multi-end knit: chosen for the balance between openness and support.
  4. Form: flat, corrugated or custom-shaped, with the corrugation matched to the stack.
  5. Size: large single pieces reduce joins inside the active area.
  6. Treatment: annealing and coating to tune springback and surface behaviour.

BVK Hydrotech’s knitted mesh

BVK Hydrotech knits single-end and multi-end structures in nickel, titanium, stainless steel and other alloys for electrolyser and fuel cell stacks. The knitted mesh range and the electrolyser solutions page set out the available structures; the nickel mesh article covers the alkaline case in more detail.

title.rendered: Choosing a Mesh Alloy for Corrosion Resistance: Stainless Steel, Nickel and Titanium

content.rendered:
Corrosion is the most common reason a metal mesh fails early. The right alloy depends on what the mesh sees, at what temperature, and for how long.

Austenitic stainless steel: 304 and 316L

Grade 304 is the general-purpose choice for clean water, food and many mild process fluids. Grade 316 adds molybdenum, which improves resistance to chlorides and many acids. The low-carbon 316L variant is preferred where the mesh is welded, because it resists sensitisation near the weld.

Higher-alloyed stainless: 904L and beyond

Where 316L is borderline, grades such as 904L offer more resistance to sulphuric acid and chlorides, at higher cost.

Nickel and nickel alloys

Pure nickel grades such as Ni 201 and Ni 202 are strong choices for caustic service, which is why they are used in alkaline electrolysis. Nickel-chromium-molybdenum alloys such as Hastelloy C-22 handle a very wide range of aggressive media, including oxidising and reducing conditions.

Titanium

Titanium forms a stable oxide film and resists chlorides, seawater and many oxidising acids. It is also light. It is the usual material for porous transport layers and current collectors in PEM electrolysers.

A quick selection guide

Service Alloys to consider
Clean water, food, mild chemicals 304, 316L
Chlorides, brine, marine 316L, 904L, titanium
Caustic and alkaline electrolyte Nickel 201 / 202
Aggressive mixed chemistry Hastelloy C-22 and similar
Acidic electrolyte, PEM cell Titanium

Treat the table as a starting point. Temperature, concentration, impurities and flow all change the real answer, so confirm against the application.

Remember the whole component

The mesh, the frame, the welds and the housing should be compatible with each other as well as with the fluid. A corrosion-proof mesh in a corroding frame is still a failed filter. See our precision mesh range for the materials we work in.

title.rendered: Pressure Drop in Metal Filter Mesh: How Wire, Opening and Open Area Interact

content.rendered:
A filter that retains the right particles but starves the process of flow has failed. Pressure drop across the element is the number that links the mesh to the rest of the system: pump size, energy cost, cleaning interval and element life.

What drives pressure drop

  • Open area. The fraction of the cloth that is open. More open area lowers resistance to flow.
  • Wire diameter. For a fixed aperture, thicker wire reduces open area and raises resistance. Thicker wire does add strength.
  • Aperture. Finer openings resist flow more, especially with viscous liquids.
  • Flow velocity. Resistance rises with velocity, so sizing the filter area is as important as choosing the mesh.
  • Fluid properties. Viscosity and temperature change how hard the fluid is to push through the same cloth.
  • Fouling. As particles collect, pressure drop climbs. The clean pressure drop is only the starting point.

Strength versus flow

The designer is balancing two demands. A strong mesh needs enough wire to withstand the differential pressure and handling. A free-flowing mesh needs enough open area. Supporting layers, pleating and corrugation let a fine, thin cloth do the filtering while a coarser backing carries the load.

Ways to lower pressure drop without losing retention

  1. Increase filter area through pleating, corrugation or a larger element, so the same flow moves more slowly through the cloth.
  2. Select the weave that gives the needed retention with the most open area.
  3. Control porosity and permeability through wire choice and mesh construction.
  4. Plan the cleaning cycle so the element works in its low-resistance range.

Verify, do not assume

Calculations get you to a shortlist. A sample tested at the real flow and with the real fluid tells you the pressure drop you will actually see. BVK Hydrotech supports prototyping and engineering optimisation for exactly this step; see R&D, CFD and prototyping and knitted mesh solutions for flow-critical parts.

title.rendered: Mesh Count vs Micron Rating: Reading Filtration Ratings Correctly

content.rendered:
Buyers often ask for a mesh “in microns”. Engineers often specify a mesh “by count”. Both are describing the same wire cloth from different angles, and mixing them up leads to the wrong filter.

Mesh count

Mesh count is the number of openings per linear inch. A higher count means more, smaller openings. It does not, on its own, tell you the opening size, because that also depends on the wire diameter used.

Aperture

Aperture is the clear distance between two adjacent wires. For a given mesh count, a thicker wire gives a smaller aperture. Aperture is the dimension that decides what can pass through.

Micron rating

A micron rating states the size of particle a filter is expected to retain. Two ideas matter here:

  • Nominal rating: a stated percentage of particles of that size are retained.
  • Absolute rating: particles above that size are retained to a defined, tested efficiency.

Always ask which one a quoted figure means, and how it was measured.

Why a micron number alone is not enough

Two filters with the same micron rating can behave very differently in service because of:

  • the open area, which sets pressure drop and flow capacity;
  • the weave, which affects how particles are held and released;
  • the way the mesh is supported, joined and sealed in the element;
  • the fluid, which may carry particles that deform, agglomerate or blind the surface.

How to specify it properly

  1. Name the particle size that must be retained and the size that may pass.
  2. State the fluid, temperature, pressure and flow.
  3. Say how the element will be cleaned or replaced.
  4. Let the supplier recommend the weave, wire and construction, and confirm with a sample.

That is the thinking behind our page on industrial filtration mesh: describe the duty, not just the micron.

title.rendered: Woven vs Knitted Metal Mesh: Differences, Applications and How to Choose

content.rendered:
Both are made from wire, and both are sold as metal mesh, but woven and knitted constructions behave very differently once they are in a stack, a housing or a separator. Understanding the difference saves a redesign later.

How woven mesh is made

Woven mesh is produced on a loom. Warp wires run along the length and weft wires cross them, locking at every intersection. Plain, twill and Dutch weaves change how tightly the wires pack and therefore how fine and how strong the finished cloth is.

What you get: a controlled, repeatable aperture, good dimensional stability and a surface that supports rated filtration and electrode work.

How knitted mesh is made

Knitted mesh is formed from interlocking loops of a single wire or several wires, in the same way a stocking is knitted. The loops can slide against each other.

What you get: a flexible, elastic and compressible structure that can be shaped into tubes, corrugated forms or large single pieces, and that holds a springy, open structure under load.

Where each one is used

Need Woven Knitted
Rated filtration and screening Preferred Less common
Electrode and catalyst support Common Common
Gas-liquid separation and demisting Less common Preferred
Elastic, compressible elements in stacks Limited Preferred
Formed parts and large single pieces Cut and joined Knitted to shape

The practical decision

  1. If the opening size must be tightly controlled, start with woven.
  2. If the mesh must flex, spring or fill a volume, start with knitted.
  3. If it must do both, talk to an engineer; hybrid constructions and surface treatments can bridge the gap.

BVK Hydrotech makes both. Explore woven mesh solutions and knitted mesh solutions, or see how they feed into industrial filtration.

title.rendered: How to Choose the Right Metal Filter Mesh for Industrial Filtration

content.rendered:
Metal filter mesh looks simple until the first project goes wrong. A mesh that retains the right particle size can still blind within a week, corrode in the process fluid or collapse under differential pressure. Choosing well means starting from the duty, not from a catalogue number.

Start with the six process inputs

Every reliable selection comes back to the same six questions.

  • Fluid type. Liquid, gas or slurry changes the weave, the wire and the construction of the element around it.
  • Particle size and load. What must be retained, how much of it arrives, and whether it is hard, soft or fibrous.
  • Operating conditions. Pressure, temperature, flow rate and whether any of them cycle.
  • Material compatibility. Chemical attack, chlorides, caustic or acid, and the temperature at which they act.
  • Required form. Sheet, roll, disc, tube, cartridge or a formed component fixes how the mesh is cut, joined and supported.
  • Service environment. Cleaning method, maintenance interval and how long the element is expected to run between changes.

Match the mesh construction to the job

Woven mesh gives a stable, repeatable opening and suits rated filtration, screening and electrode support. Knitted mesh is flexible and compressible, which suits gas-liquid separation and elastic elements. If you are unsure which route fits, read our guide to woven versus knitted metal mesh.

Pick the alloy for the fluid, not the budget

Stainless steel covers many duties, nickel alloys handle caustic service, and titanium resists chlorides. A cheaper alloy that corrodes in service costs far more than the difference at purchase. Our alloy selection guide sets out how the main families behave.

Think about cleaning and life from day one

A mesh that can be back-flushed, ultrasonically cleaned or replaced as a cartridge changes the economics of a filtration line. Decide how the element will be maintained before you fix the opening, because a finer opening rewards cleaning discipline and punishes neglect.

Confirm against the real application

Published ratings are a starting point. The final specification should be confirmed against the actual fluid, particles and installation, ideally with a sample run. This is also why a filtration supplier should ask you questions before quoting.
